name: Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling
intent: Handle more load either by making one machine bigger (scale up) or by adding more machines (scale out), and know what each choice costs.
scenario: A web app runs on one small server that handled 80 requests per second comfortably. Traffic is heading toward 250 requests per second and beyond.
problem: Every machine has a ceiling. When demand passes it, requests slow down, queue and fail. You have two ways to raise the ceiling, and they behave very differently on cost, risk, complexity and how far they can go.

howItWorks.title: Vertical scaling: a bigger machine
howItWorks.text: Add CPU, memory or faster disks to the same server. The application does not change, which makes it the quickest fix. But machine size has a hard limit, prices rise faster than capacity at the top end, and resizing often means downtime.

howItWorks.title: Horizontal scaling: more machines
howItWorks.text: Run several copies of the service behind a load balancer. Capacity grows roughly in step with the number of machines, and there is no single machine to fall over. The price is that the application must work when requests land on different servers.

howItWorks.title: Stateless services scale out easily
howItWorks.text: If a server keeps no per-user data in its own memory, any server can answer any request. Move sessions and files to shared stores (a cache, a database, object storage) and the web tier becomes trivially scalable.

howItWorks.title: The data tier is the hard part
howItWorks.text: Databases hold state, so they cannot simply be cloned. They scale up first, then use replication (extra copies that serve reads) for reads and sharding (splitting the data across several databases) for writes. This is why teams often scale web servers out and databases up for as long as they can.

howItWorks.title: Elasticity: scale automatically
howItWorks.text: Autoscaling adds servers when utilisation passes a threshold and removes them when load falls. Horizontal scaling makes this possible, so you pay for roughly what you use.

pros: Vertical: simple, no code changes, no distributed-systems problems
Horizontal: nearly unlimited headroom and cost grows about linearly
Horizontal: survives the loss of a machine, and enables rolling deploys
Horizontal: pairs well with autoscaling for uneven traffic
cons: Vertical: hard ceiling, steep cost at the top, and one machine is a single point of failure (if it dies, everything is down)
Vertical: resizing may need a restart
Horizontal: needs a load balancer and stateless services or shared state
Horizontal: more machines to deploy, monitor and keep consistent
whenToUse: Scale up first when you are small, the app is stateful, or the database is the bottleneck
Scale out for web and API tiers, bursty traffic, and anything that must stay up through failures
Do both: bigger database, many web servers
whenNotToUse: Do not scale out a service that keeps important state in local memory without fixing that first
Do not keep scaling up past the point where the next size costs several times more for a small gain
Do not add servers when the real bottleneck is a slow query or a single locked resource
pitfalls: Scaling the wrong tier: adding web servers does nothing if the database is saturated
Sticky sessions (always sending a user to the same server) or local files quietly preventing horizontal scaling
Treating one huge machine as safe because it never fails, until it does
Autoscaling too slowly for a sudden spike, or flapping up and down

roles.label: Load balancer
roles.description: Spreads requests when there are several servers.

roles.label: Server
roles.description: A machine with a fixed request capacity.

quiz.question: A stateless API runs on one 4-core server at 95% CPU, with traffic expected to triple. The database on a separate server sits at 15% CPU. The business also requires that the API survive the loss of any single server. What is the best next step?
options: Move the API to a server with 3 times the cores, which keeps one machine and avoids a load balancer
Run several API servers behind a load balancer, which also removes the single point of failure
Shard the database across several servers before touching the API tier, to cut the load on the database
Add read replicas to the database so the API can send reads elsewhere
quiz.explanation: The saturated tier is the stateless API, and scale-out also meets the availability requirement. A single bigger server would still be a single point of failure, and the database has plenty of headroom, so sharding it or adding read replicas would fix nothing.

quiz.question: A site has 6 web servers at 20% CPU and one database at 95% CPU, mostly from write-heavy queries. The database runs on a mid-size instance, and the next size up doubles its capacity for twice the price. The team plans to add 6 more web servers. What is the best step now?
options: Add the 6 web servers anyway, because more front-end capacity lets the database queue work more smoothly
Shard the database into several write nodes now, before any larger instance is tried
Turn on autoscaling for the web tier so the database load is spread across servers
Move the database to the next larger instance and look at slow queries first
quiz.explanation: Scaling the wrong tier does nothing: the web servers are idle and extra ones only send more queries to a saturated database. Scaling the database up is the cheapest first move, autoscaling the web tier does not lower database load, and sharding is a large complexity step that is not yet justified.

quiz.question: A company adds a second app server behind a load balancer. Users are logged out at random, because login sessions live in each server's memory. The app will later autoscale and must not log users out when a server is removed. What is the best fix?
options: Turn on sticky sessions so each user always lands on the server that holds their session
Move the app back to one larger server, since sessions only work on a single machine
Move sessions into a shared store such as Redis, so any server can answer any user
Lengthen the session timeout so a session survives long enough to be found on the other server
quiz.explanation: Shared session storage makes the web tier stateless, so servers can be added or removed freely. Sticky sessions keep the state on one server, so removing it still logs out its users. One server gives up the autoscaling goal, and a longer timeout does not move the session data to the other server.
